turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mr Kulkarni, come in, sit. Sorry about the wait, the token system was stuck again.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ugh. I was outside since forty minutes. I am tired, doctor, please can we do this quickly.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He hardly slept, so his mood is off. I am Sunita, his wife. I will fill the gaps if he snaps.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not snapping. I can answer. Let me talk.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course. In your own words, what did you come for today.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): This left hand. It is still weak. That is the reason.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): The mild stroke, how long ago are we now.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months. Well, actually I can't remember the exact date, about three months.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And day to day, what can the hand manage.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Slight weakness only, same three months. I can hold a cup. Shirt buttons take ages, the fingers don't close properly.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): You have high blood pressure as well, long standing, yes?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, the BP is there. Eight years, or nine, I can't place the year. It is just ongoing.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, by evening that hand is almost useless. And when he is tired his speech goes slurred. Every night I notice it.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): It does not. My speech is fine. She exaggerates. The hand is slight weakness, not useless.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am not going to pretend those two accounts match. Tell me about walking.
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He drags the left foot. From the door to the gate itself he is very slow, I don't like it.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not drag the foot. I walk to the milk booth every morning. I am slow, that is all.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fall since the stroke?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any choking, trouble swallowing food or water?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, on walking or at rest?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the hand painful?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. Weak, not painful.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Numbness, pins and needles in the fingers?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Breathlessness?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Coming back to the blood pressure. Any headache with it?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. A dull headache in the evening. Not daily.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he is worn out. After lunch he just sits and stares.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Ya, that part is true. Since the stroke I am tired, energy is less. Don't look so surprised.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. The tablets, tell me what you swallow, dose if you know it.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Aspirin a hundred milligrams, no, they reduced it, seventy five milligrams every morning, after the stroke. Atorvastin forty milligrams at night for the cholesterol. And one amlodipine tablet, five milligram, morning, for the BP.
[SEG0036] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The night one, the atorvastin, if dinner is late he skips it. Two or three nights a week it is still in the strip.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Not two or three. Maybe once. I take my tablets. She counts them like a cashier.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hmm, so whether the statin is taken as prescribed, I actually don't know. I won't put a false number in the note. Any other medicine, diabetes or another thinner?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Only those three. Please don't start a fourth, I am fed up.

[SEG0040] person_4 (NURSE): Sorry, doctor, vitals for him. Today's pressure is one oh nine over seventy seven, and the weight is sixty four kilos. Pulse seventy two, ah sorry, that seventy two is the March column, pulse today is seventy eight.
[SEG0041] person_4 (NURSE): Last time in March you were sixty eight kilos. Your last pressure was one forty.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. Today I am keeping one oh nine over seventy seven, pulse seventy eight, and sixty four kilos. The March weight and that old pressure I am leaving out. One oh nine is a bit soft on the amlodipine, but I am not changing the dose off a single reading.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me see, squeeze my fingers. Left grip is weaker than the right, and there is no facial droop. Your speech just now is clear, I am not hearing any slurring in the room.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thinking it through, this could be the old stroke still in the hand, it could be neck changes adding a bit, and I am not going to conclude it is a fresh stroke. Not today, and I am not booking an MRI.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is residual weakness of the left hand from the mild stroke. I cannot rule out a cervical contribution, so that stays as a possibility.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I want a fasting lipid profile and a blood sugar, to see how the cholesterol tablet is doing. They are booked downstairs, you can give the sample before you go.

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Continue the aspirin seventy five in the morning, atorvastatin forty at night, and amlodipine five in the morning. Keep walking daily. Please try not to skip the statin even if dinner runs late.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will see you in six weeks. And if the weakness suddenly increases or the speech slurs in the daytime, come the same day, don't wait.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, fine. I am too tired to argue the rest. The parking chap took eighty rupees, that annoyed me more than the hand.
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I will bring the tablet strip next time so you can see the statin.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): That would help. Take the lab form from the desk, both of you, and go easy today.

spec.situation: Patient three months after a mild stroke with a spouse; slight weakness in the left hand; takes aspirin, atorvastatin and an amlodipine tablet; blood pressure read aloud; walking and speech discussed.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

bad.reason: Patient said 'Not really,' not a clear complete absence.
Patient said 'Not really' painful; not a fully unequivocal absence.
Drug, dose, timing supported, but current use is uncertain due to reported skipped doses.
